messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Thomas Hayes, a fifty-year-old European American psychologist, had built his career on helping clients navigate crisis, but his own world fractured three years ago when he was raped in a narrow, rain-slicked alley behind a downtown bar. The attacker had pinned him against the damp brick wall, his breath heavy with cheap whiskey, and as the struggle ended, Thomas lay trapped on the pavement while distant police sirens wailed down the street. That precise convergence of sensory details permanently fused to his nervous system. In the months that followed, Thomas found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it, a defensive reflex that left him with a chilling gap in his narrative. Instead of a coherent story, he was left with the quiet conviction that he could not put the frightening event into words. Sometimes, in the isolation of his home office, he felt the full emotional intensity of the violation without any clear image or memory of it, a raw, wordless panic that would tighten his chest and leave him gripping his desk until his fingers ached. When Thomas encountered his triggers in his daily practice, the sensory intrusion directly fed his worsening self-appraisals. Whenever the faint scent of bourbon drifted from a colleague’s breakroom coffee mug, or a fire engine’s siren vibrated through his office window, he would immediately feel emotionally numb, as if a switch had been thrown inside him. This sudden hollowing sensation cemented his belief that he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him as a clinician, while simultaneously deepening his sense of dehumanization until he felt like an object, not like a person. These negative appraisals actively dictated how his mind handled the trauma. His conviction of internal deadness and professional incapacity triggered a rigid shutdown, causing him to push the memory away before he could fully recall it during clinical supervision. Simultaneously, his internal narrative of objectification amplified his environmental vigilance. Feeling stripped of autonomy made him hyper-aware of sensory cues, so the auditory ping of a siren or the sight of a liquor bottle on a shelf would instantly heighten his discomfort, leaving him feeling uncomfortably exposed and on edge. The fragmented nature of his recall further entrenched his worst fears. When the nonverbal emotional intensity would surface without a clear image, Thomas interpreted the wordless panic as proof that he was emotionally dead inside. This misinterpretation solidified his appraisal of dehumanization, creating a reciprocal tightening. Over the past year, this pattern systematically dismantled his routine. He avoided driving past his practice’s adjacent parking garage, stopped attending his clinic’s monthly staff gatherings, and spent his evenings sitting in a darkened study, afraid to turn on the overhead lights. His wife, Elena, watched him retreat into a shell of quiet withdrawal, noting how he flinched when she returned from grocery shopping carrying a six-pack of beer, and how he had lost the engaged presence that once characterized their marriage. It was the sheer exhaustion of maintaining this silent perimeter that finally drove Thomas to schedule an intake. He was terrified that his professional training had been completely hollowed out by the assault, that his conviction of incapacity was a permanent sentence rather than a treatable symptom. Walking into the clinic, he braced himself against the sterile air and the distant hum of traffic, hoping against his own rigid expectations that he might learn to inhabit his body again without the constant alarm. He sought help not to relive the alley, but to reclaim the clinician he used to be before the trauma rewrote his reality.
